entry.title: Virtual simulation of the 7.9M 1906 San Francisco earthquake spotlights human behavioral response

media:group.media:title: Virtual simulation of the 7.9M 1906 San Francisco earthquake spotlights human behavioral response
media:group.media:description: UC Berkeley researchers are seeking to better understand people’s earthquake risk perception with the goal of improving earthquake safety. They recently set out to create an immersive representation of an indoor earthquake by synchronizing the shaking of the Shake House (https://www.calacademy.org/exhibits/california-state-of-nature/shake-house), an earthquake simulator at the California Academy of Sciences, with a virtual reality environment they developed. So when test subjects saw things falling in virtual reality, the physics corresponded to the shaking they felt. During the experiment, test subjects wore VR headsets that recorded their gaze, and they could press a button on the VR controller whenever they felt at risk of being injured. “For earthquake engineers, this gives us a new way to go beyond computational models and study how people perceive risk and make decisions as earthquakes unfold,” said civil engineering professor Luis Ceferino. “Getting answers would give us more information to develop policy, recommendations and guidance for what to do when there is an earthquake to further reduce people’s risk of injury.” (Video courtesy the researchers)

entry.title: UC Berkeley Ph.D. Student Combats Foodborne Illness with Electronic Nose

media:group.media:title: UC Berkeley Ph.D. Student Combats Foodborne Illness with Electronic Nose
media:group.media:description:
How to win first place at UC Berkeley’s Grad Slam? Follow your next-gen electronic nose.
At least that’s what worked for Carla Bassil, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering and computer sciences.
She is working to improve food safety, one gas sensor chip at a time.
This multi-modal gas sensing technology could sniff out spoilage, contamination and unsafe compounds in our food — long before our human noses could detect any defects.
It’s an engineering feat that could prevent the food-borne illnesses that result in 128,000 hospitalizations and 3,000 deaths in America each year.
Read our profile on Bassil’s research: bit.ly/4uNCEQk
Audio taken from Bassil’s Grad Slam presentation. (UC Berkeley Graduate Division / YouTube)

entry.title: Lessons Learned in Aerospace Engineering at UC Berkeley 🚀

media:group.media:title: Lessons Learned in Aerospace Engineering at UC Berkeley 🚀
media:group.media:description:
#DidYouKnow This year, Berkeley Engineering is sending off our first cohort of our new aerospace engineering program at tomorrow’s commencement ceremony! 🐻🎓
To celebrate this milestone, we asked members of the graduating class: "What was your biggest learning lesson in aerospace engineering at UC Berkeley?"
Hear it from our grads:
Madeleine Bardy: “My biggest learnings came from participating in clubs and organizations, where I learned to challenge complex engineering problems in interdisciplinary teams.
I was a part of the team that sent Uc Berkeley’s first student-build liquid propellant rocket to space and built Berkeley’s first regeneratively cooled liquid-bipropellant rocket engine.
These are things that engineers in industry haven’t even had the chance to experience. And I’m really grateful to the aerospace program here.”
Jordan Kam: “It’s just how rich the research community and opportunities there are.
As an undergraduate student here at Berkeley, for the past three years, I’ve been doing research in the Berkeley AI Research Lab with aerospace-affiliated faculty.
Through these opportunities, I’ve been able to do hands-on research and publications and travel the world to present some of my research.”
Aaron Bush Wegulo: “One of the biggest learning lessons in aerospace engineering has been understanding the power of resilience and community.
Aerospace engineering is a demanding field. There are moments when the workload is demanding as well.
Understanding that during these moments, these difficult moments, that’s when growth happens. That’s when you choose to pick yourself, when you choose to push yourself.
Andrew Ji: “It’s the importance of first principles thinking. I think the coursework here was actually really great about preparing us to do those kinds of things.
I got to explore anything and everything from embedded systems to compressible flow to robotics.
I thought that gave me a lot of breadth to pull from whenever I tackle engineering problems.”

entry.title: A Day in the Life of an Engineering Student at UC Berkeley!

media:group.media:title: A Day in the Life of an Engineering Student at UC Berkeley!
media:group.media:description:
Join Gauri Mutha (B.S.’27 EECS, MSE) on a day in her life as an engineering student at UC Berkeley!
She adds: “As an international student at UC Berkeley pursuing electrical engineering and computer sciences as well as materials science and engineering, every day here feels like proof of how far I’ve come and how much this place has given me.
Berkeley has challenged me in the best ways — through rigorous classes, research opportunities, late nights in labs and conversations with people who constantly inspire me to think bigger.
Coming here meant building a life far from home, learning to navigate a new country and finding my place in one of the most intellectually exciting communities in the world.
Berkeley has given me more than an education; it has given me courage, independence, friendships, purpose and the confidence to dream beyond what I once thought was possible.
I’m grateful for the professors, classmates, mentors and friends who have shaped my journey and made this campus feel like home. Every day here reminds me that growth is not always easy, but it is always worth it. Proud to be a Bear. Go Bears!"
Want to share your journey at Berkeley Engineering? Reach us at coesocial@berkeley.edu!
#BerkeleyEngineering #UCBerkeley #EngineeringLife #EngineeringStudents #youtubeshorts
